structure.title: Volume I, Part 1 · Start in a township
structure.text: Tocqueville traces power from local offices through state government to the federal Constitution. A citizen who helps decide the maintenance of a road learns habits of public business that a fine description of national institutions could easily miss.

structure.title: Volume I, Part 2 · Ask who can withstand a majority
structure.text: Juries, newspapers, associations and religion enter the account as forces that shape public power. The discussion of Indigenous peoples and slavery brings into view lives whose conditions sit uneasily beside the promise of democratic equality.

structure.title: Volume II · Follow equality into private life
structure.text: The inquiry moves into reading habits, ambition, work, families and friendship. Tocqueville imagines citizens absorbed in their own small circles growing willing to entrust more of their common affairs to a solicitous central authority.

people.name: Equality of conditions
people.role: The great change Tocqueville thinks he sees
people.text: The phrase concerns the erosion of inherited social orders. Great disparities of wealth and power remain visible in the America he visits, and his own account repeatedly tests how far the phrase can travel.

people.name: Associations
people.text: A local project can draw strangers into writing rules, raising funds and arguing over a decision. Tocqueville cares about the capacities left behind once the immediate business is finished.

people.name: The majority
people.role: A power with few visible officers
people.text: Its influence reaches beyond legislation. A dissenter might legally publish an opinion and still discover that every respectable door has closed, an outcome Tocqueville asks the reader to count among political pressures.

context.title: A French visitor's question
context.text: Tocqueville is writing with France's political upheavals in mind. American arrangements interest him partly because they suggest several possible futures for societies losing their old aristocratic order. His comparisons carry the assumptions of that vantage point.

context.title: Laws, geography and customs
context.text: Similar written rules can work differently where people have acquired different habits of trusting, meeting and taking responsibility. Tocqueville repeatedly moves among these levels when he tries to explain why a particular institution survives.

notice.text: Watch the citizen become a juror.
notice.why: Jury service teaches people to weigh evidence, follow a procedure and share responsibility for a binding judgment. An institution designed to decide a case may also educate the people deciding it.

notice.text: Mark the move from a report to a forecast.
notice.why: An observation about the America Tocqueville saw can become a prediction about what democratic peoples in general will want. The second claim asks considerably more of the evidence than the first.

opening: Tocqueville arrives in America to study prisons and becomes absorbed by a much larger experiment: a society in which equality is changing how people think, associate, and govern. He admires the energy, then notices the pressure to agree and the isolation that can accompany independence. Democracy may free people from inherited masters while making them unusually vulnerable to public opinion. His travels turn into an investigation of the habits and institutions that allow a population to remain free after it has become politically equal.
